claim: Chronic ISO infusion significantly increased heart weight/tibia length (HW/TL) ratio in mice.
source: Chronic ISO infusion significantly increased heart weight/tibia length (HW/TL) ratio as well as left ventricular wall thickness, which is an indicator of cardiac hypertrophy, while reducing the ejection fraction of heart (Figure 1A–C), suggesting that ISO-infusion causes adverse cardiac remodeling and contractile dysfunction in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C from ISO-infused mice compared to vehicle controls.

claim: Chronic ISO infusion significantly increased left ventricular wall thickness in mice.
source: Chronic ISO infusion significantly increased heart weight/tibia length (HW/TL) ratio as well as left ventricular wall thickness, which is an indicator of cardiac hypertrophy, while reducing the ejection fraction of heart (Figure 1A–C), suggesting that ISO-infusion causes adverse cardiac remodeling and contractile dysfunction in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B from ISO-infused mice compared to vehicle controls.

claim: Chronic ISO infusion reduced the ejection fraction of heart in mice.
source: Chronic ISO infusion significantly increased heart weight/tibia length (HW/TL) ratio as well as left ventricular wall thickness, which is an indicator of cardiac hypertrophy, while reducing the ejection fraction of heart (Figure 1A–C), suggesting that ISO-infusion causes adverse cardiac remodeling and contractile dysfunction in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C from ISO-infused mice compared to vehicle controls.

claim: ISO-infusion causes adverse cardiac remodeling and contractile dysfunction in mice.
source: Chronic ISO infusion significantly increased heart weight/tibia length (HW/TL) ratio as well as left ventricular wall thickness, which is an indicator of cardiac hypertrophy, while reducing the ejection fraction of heart (Figure 1A–C), suggesting that ISO-infusion causes adverse cardiac remodeling and contractile dysfunction in mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of increased HW/TL ratio, increased wall thickness, and reduced ejection fraction shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: GSK3β activity is reduced in hypertrophic hearts.
source: Previous studies indicate that GSK3β activity is reduced in hypertrophic hearts (Sugden et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Sugden et al., 2008.

claim: Activity of GSK3β was significantly low in ISO-infused heart samples.
source: Our results revealed that activity of GSK3β was significantly low in ISO-infused heart samples (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: β-catenin levels were high in ISO-infused hearts.
source: Moreover, the levels of β-catenin, a GSK3 target transcription factor, which degrade after phosphorylation by GSK3 (Liu et al., 2002), was high in ISO-infused hearts (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Liu et al., 2002.

claim: β-catenin degrades after phosphorylation by GSK3.
source: Moreover, the levels of β-catenin, a GSK3 target transcription factor, which degrade after phosphorylation by GSK3 (Liu et al., 2002), was high in ISO-infused hearts (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2002.

claim: Acetylation of GSK3β was markedly increased in the heart samples of ISO-infused mice.
source: Interestingly, we found markedly increased acetylation of GSK3β in the heart samples of ISO-infused mice (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blotting data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: There were no marked changes in Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β in chronic ISO-infused heart samples.
source: However, we did not see marked changes in Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β in the chronic ISO-infused heart samples (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Total protein levels and Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β were not changed in the heart after pressure overload or myocardial infarction.
source: Our results were consistent with previous observations, where the total protein levels and Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β were not changed in the heart after pressure overload or myocardial infarction (Zhai et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhai et al., 2007.

claim: GSK3β Ser9 phosphorylation was unchanged in the heart of mice-treated with ISO.
source: Similarly, the GSK3β Ser9 phosphorylation was unchanged in the heart of mice-treated with ISO (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: The reduced activity of GSK3β found in chronic ISO-infused hearts is correlated with increased lysine acetylation, but not with inhibitory Ser9 phosphorylation.
source: These findings indicate that the reduced activity of GSK3β found in chronic ISO-infused hearts is correlated with increased lysine acetylation, but not with inhibitory Ser nine phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of increased acetylation, unchanged Ser9 phosphorylation, and reduced activity observed in ISO-infused hearts.

claim: Reduced levels of Tyr216 phosphorylation of GSK3β were observed in ISO-infused heart samples.
source: Furthermore, we observed reduced levels of Tyr216 phosphorylation of GSK3β in ISO-infused heart samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression levels of SIRT2 reduced in ISO-treated heart samples.
source: The expression levels of SIRT2 also reduced in the ISO-treated heart samples (Figure 1E), suggesting that acetylation of GSK3β may be linked to reduced levels of SIRT2 deacetylase.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Acetylation of GSK3β may be linked to reduced levels of SIRT2 deacetylase.
source: The expression levels of SIRT2 also reduced in the ISO-treated heart samples (Figure 1E), suggesting that acetylation of GSK3β may be linked to reduced levels of SIRT2 deacetylase.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the correlation between reduced SIRT2 levels and increased GSK3β acetylation.

claim: p300 binds to GSK3β.
source: Our immunoprecipitation experiments showed that p300 binds to GSK3β (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: p300 co-localizes with GSK3β.
source: Further confocal microscopy analysis indicated that p300 co-localizes with GSK3β (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: p300 binds to GSK3β directly in an in vitro reaction.
source: Our results indicate that p300 binds to GSK3β directly in an in vitro reaction (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 1I using recombinant purified proteins.

claim: Depletion of p300 resulted in reduced levels of acetylation of GSK3β.
source: We found that the depletion of p300 resulted in reduced levels of acetylation, although the effect is not robust, it increased the activity of GSK3β, as suggested by increase in GS phosphorylation (Figure 1J–1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blotting data shown in Figure 1J-L from p300-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of p300 increased the activity of GSK3β.
source: We found that the depletion of p300 resulted in reduced levels of acetylation, although the effect is not robust, it increased the activity of GSK3β, as suggested by increase in GS phosphorylation (Figure 1J–1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data showing increased GS phosphorylation in Figure 1J-L from p300-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of p300 markedly increased the phosphorylation of Tyr216, but not Ser9 in GSK3β.
source: Interestingly, depletion of p300 markedly increased the phosphorylation of Tyr216, but not Ser9 in GSK3β (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1J from p300-depleted cells.

claim: Overexpression of p300 significantly increased acetylation of GSK3β.
source: We found significantly increased acetylation of GSK3β, which is associated with reduced activity of GSK3β in p300 overexpressing cells (Figure 1M, N and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1M from p300 overexpressing cells.

claim: Overexpression of p300 is associated with reduced activity of GSK3β.
source: We found significantly increased acetylation of GSK3β, which is associated with reduced activity of GSK3β in p300 overexpressing cells (Figure 1M, N and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1N and O from p300 overexpressing cells.

claim: Overexpression of p300 markedly reduced the Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β.
source: Moreover, overexpression of p300 markedly reduced the Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1M from p300 overexpressing cells.

claim: p300-mediated acetylation significantly impairs kinase activity of GSK3β.
source: Next, we tested the enzymatic activity of acetylated GSK3β in vitro and found that p300-mediated acetylation significantly impairs kinase activity of GSK3β (Figure 1P).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: p300-mediated acetylation might influence the phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216 residue, but not Ser9, to inhibit the enzymatic activity.
source: These findings suggest that p300-mediated acetylation might influence the phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216 residue, but not Ser9, to inhibit the enzymatic activity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that p300 affects Tyr216 but not Ser9 phosphorylation and reduces GSK3β activity.

claim: K150 and K183 are acetylation sites in GSK3β.
source: Therefore, we performed tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analysis of GSK3β and identified two lysine residues, K150 and K183, as acetylation sites in GSK3β (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by tandem mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: K183 is located in the vicinity of nucleotide-binding pocket of GSK3β.
source: While K183 is located in the vicinity of nucleotide-binding pocket of GSK3β, K150 is located on the surface away from both nucleotide-binding pocket as well as substrate-binding region (Figure 2B I-III).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: K150 is located on the surface away from both nucleotide-binding pocket as well as substrate-binding region.
source: While K183 is located in the vicinity of nucleotide-binding pocket of GSK3β, K150 is located on the surface away from both nucleotide-binding pocket as well as substrate-binding region (Figure 2B I-III).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The side-chain of K183 residue is proximal to the magnesium ion of the adenosine di-phosphate nucleotide.
source: Interestingly, the side-chain of K183 residue is proximal to the magnesium ion of the adenosine di-phosphate nucleotide (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The addition of the acetylated group to the NZ atom of K183 side-chain may result in destabilization of Mg2+ from ADP.
source: The addition of the acetylated group to the NZ atom of K183 side-chain may result in destabilization of Mg2+ from ADP (Figure 2B II-IV).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural modeling shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The acetylation of K183 side-chain may reduce the affinity of adenosine tri-phosphate (ATP) nucleotide to the binding pocket by interfering with its magnesium cofactor.
source: Overall, in-silico analysis suggests that the acetylation of K183 side-chain may reduce the affinity of adenosine tri-phosphate (ATP) nucleotide to the binding pocket by interfering with its magnesium cofactor.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on in silico analysis and structural modeling.

claim: Acetylation would hinder both the adenosine binding as well as prevent stable interactions of the negatively charged phosphates with the protein.
source: Our results suggest that the acetylation would hinder both the adenosine binding as well as prevent stable interactions of the negatively charged phosphates with the protein.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation results showing increased distances between ADP and protein residues in the acetylated mutant.

claim: The acetylation of K183 would destabilize the binding of the adenine nucleotide to the pocket of GSK3β.
source: Collectively, we propose that the acetylation of K183 would destabilize the binding of the adenine nucleotide to the pocket of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular dynamics simulation results and ATP binding assays.

claim: GSK3β-K183 mutations significantly reduced binding of ATP to GSK3β, when compared to wild type GSK3β.
source: GSK3β-K183 mutations significantly reduced binding of ATP to GSK3β, when compared to wild type GSK3β (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP binding assay data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: K183 is critically important for ATP binding to GSK3β.
source: These findings provided strong evidence that K183 is critically important for ATP binding to GSK3β and any modifications, including acetylation might affect its ATP-binding ability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ATP binding assay results showing reduced ATP binding in K183 mutants.

claim: Any modifications of K183, including acetylation might affect its ATP-binding ability.
source: These findings provided strong evidence that K183 is critically important for ATP binding to GSK3β and any modifications, including acetylation might affect its ATP-binding ability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ATP binding assay results showing reduced ATP binding in K183 mutants.

claim: Mutation of K183 to either arginine or glutamine drastically reduced the catalytic activity toward a glycogen synthase peptide.
source: Our results indicate that mutation of K183 to either arginine or glutamine drastically reduced the catalytic activity toward a glycogen synthase peptide (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Mutation of K150 had no effect on GSK3β activity.
source: Mutation of K150, which is less conserved among species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and exhibited low stoichiometry of acetylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), had no effect on GSK3β activity (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 2L and supplementary figures.

claim: K183 is critical for the functionality of GSK3β.
source: It is interesting to note that mutation of K183 to either K183R or K183Q, reduced the catalytic activity more than four folds, indicating that K183 is critical for the functionality of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the kinase assay results showing >4-fold reduction in activity with K183 mutations.

claim: K183 is an important residue for ATP binding and the catalytic activity of GSK3β.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that K183 is an important residue for ATP binding and the catalytic activity of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of ATP binding assays and kinase activity assays.

claim: SIRT2 overexpression markedly reduced the acetylation of GSK3β.
source: Our results suggest that SIRT2 overexpression markedly reduced the acetylation of GSK3β, while increasing its activity against glycogen synthase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIRT2 overexpression increased GSK3β activity against glycogen synthase.
source: Our results suggest that SIRT2 overexpression markedly reduced the acetylation of GSK3β, while increasing its activity against glycogen synthase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIRT2 overexpression increased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216.
source: However, we found increased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SIRT3 is capable of deacetylating GSK3β and enhancing its catalytic activity.
source: Consistent with our previous work (Sundaresan et al., 2016), we found SIRT3 to be capable of deacetylating GSK3β and enhancing its catalytic activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Acetylation of GSK3β was markedly increased in SIRT2-KO hearts.
source: As expected, we found markedly increased acetylation of GSK3β in SIRT2-KO hearts (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blotting data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: SIRT2 interacts with GSK3β.
source: We found that SIRT2 interacts with GSK3β (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Recombinant purified GSK3β is capable of binding to SIRT2 in vitro.
source: We also found that recombinant purified GSK3β is capable of binding to SIRT2 in vitro, suggesting direct interaction between both proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is direct interaction between GSK3β and SIRT2.
source: We also found that recombinant purified GSK3β is capable of binding to SIRT2 in vitro, suggesting direct interaction between both proteins (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro binding assay using recombinant purified proteins.

claim: WT SIRT2, but not catalytic mutant-SIRT2 markedly reduced the acetylation status of GSK3β in an NAD+-dependent manner.
source: Western blotting analysis indicated WT, but not catalytic mutant-SIRT2 markedly reduced the acetylation status of GSK3β in an NAD+-dependent manner (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylation assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SIRT2 is a GSK3β deacetylase.
source: These findings indicate that SIRT2 is a GSK3β deacetylase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro deacetylation assay results.

claim: Acetylation significantly reduced the activity of GSK3β.
source: Results indicated that acetylation significantly reduced the activity of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Incubation of acetylated-GSK3β with wild type SIRT2 restored the activity of GSK3β in a NAD+-dependent manner.
source: However, incubation of acetylated-GSK3β with wild type, but not SIRT2-H187Y catalytic inactive mutant of SIRT2 restored the activity of GSK3β in a NAD+-dependent manner (Figure 3F), suggesting that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation increases GSK3β activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SIRT2-mediated deacetylation increases GSK3β activity.
source: However, incubation of acetylated-GSK3β with wild type, but not SIRT2-H187Y catalytic inactive mutant of SIRT2 restored the activity of GSK3β in a NAD+-dependent manner (Figure 3F), suggesting that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation increases GSK3β activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro kinase assay results showing restored activity after SIRT2 treatment.

claim: SIRT2 depletion increases the cellular global lysine acetylation.
source: SIRT2 depletion increases the cellular global lysine acetylation and the acetylation of GSK3β (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: SIRT2 depletion increases the acetylation of GSK3β.
source: SIRT2 depletion increases the cellular global lysine acetylation and the acetylation of GSK3β (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GSK3β-specific phosphorylation of glycogen synthase was reduced in SIRT2-depleted cardiomyocytes.
source: Moreover, GSK3β-specific phosphorylation of glycogen synthase and β-catenin was reduced in SIRT2-depleted cardiomyocytes, which is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GSK3β-specific phosphorylation of β-catenin was reduced in SIRT2-depleted cardiomyocytes.
source: Moreover, GSK3β-specific phosphorylation of glycogen synthase and β-catenin was reduced in SIRT2-depleted cardiomyocytes, which is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Reduced phosphorylation of glycogen synthase in SIRT2-depleted cardiomyocytes is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β.
source: Moreover, GSK3β-specific phosphorylation of glycogen synthase and β-catenin was reduced in SIRT2-depleted cardiomyocytes, which is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Reduced phosphorylation of glycogen synthase was observed in SIRT2-deficient heart samples.
source: To further validate the results in vivo, we tested the phosphorylation of glycogen synthase in SIRT2-deficient heart samples, and observed reduced phosphorylation of glycogen synthase, which is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β in SIRT2-KO hearts (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Reduced phosphorylation of glycogen synthase in SIRT2-KO hearts is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β.
source: To further validate the results in vivo, we tested the phosphorylation of glycogen synthase in SIRT2-deficient heart samples, and observed reduced phosphorylation of glycogen synthase, which is associated with reduced Tyr216, but not Ser9 phosphorylation of GSK3β in SIRT2-KO hearts (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Significantly reduced activity of GSK3β toward a peptide of glycogen synthase was observed in SIRT2-deficient hearts.
source: Consistent with our findings, we observed significantly reduced activity of GSK3β toward a peptide of glycogen synthase (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The protein levels of β-catenin are high in SIRT2-KO heart lysates.
source: Our results suggest that the protein levels of β-catenin are high in SIRT2-KO heart lysates, while the GSK3 target phosphorylation of β-catenin was decreased drastically (Figure 3H), indicating that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation might control the kinase activity of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The GSK3 target phosphorylation of β-catenin was decreased drastically in SIRT2-KO heart lysates.
source: Our results suggest that the protein levels of β-catenin are high in SIRT2-KO heart lysates, while the GSK3 target phosphorylation of β-catenin was decreased drastically (Figure 3H), indicating that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation might control the kinase activity of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: SIRT2-mediated deacetylation might control the kinase activity of GSK3β.
source: Our results suggest that the protein levels of β-catenin are high in SIRT2-KO heart lysates, while the GSK3 target phosphorylation of β-catenin was decreased drastically (Figure 3H), indicating that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation might control the kinase activity of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SIRT2 deficiency leads to increased β-catenin levels and decreased phosphorylation.

claim: Treatment of cells with AGK2 enhanced the acetylation of tubulin.
source: Treatment of cells with a SIRT2 inhibitor (AGK2) enhanced the acetylation of tubulin, a well-accepted target of SIRT2, and the acetylation of GSK3β, while decreasing its activity against glycogen synthase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment of cells with AGK2 enhanced the acetylation of GSK3β.
source: Treatment of cells with a SIRT2 inhibitor (AGK2) enhanced the acetylation of tubulin, a well-accepted target of SIRT2, and the acetylation of GSK3β, while decreasing its activity against glycogen synthase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment of cells with AGK2 decreased GSK3β activity against glycogen synthase.
source: Treatment of cells with a SIRT2 inhibitor (AGK2) enhanced the acetylation of tubulin, a well-accepted target of SIRT2, and the acetylation of GSK3β, while decreasing its activity against glycogen synthase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: AGK2 treatment decreased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216.
source: However, we found decreased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: AGK2 treatment had no effect on subcellular distribution of GSK3β.
source: Interestingly, AGK2 treatment had no effect on subcellular distribution of the GSK3β (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: WT and K183 mutants of GSK3β exhibited cytoplasmic localization.
source: As expected, the results suggest that the WT and K183 mutants of GSK3β exhibited cytoplasmic localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Change in the activity of GSK3β is not associated with its localization.
source: These results indicate that change in the activity of GSK3β is not associated with its localization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that K183 mutants with different activities have the same localization.

claim: There was no difference in expression levels of any other sirtuin isoforms in SIRT2-deficient mice heart samples.
source: However, we found no difference in expression levels of any other sirtuin isoforms in SIRT2-deficient mice heart samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: GSK3β K183 residue is acetylated.
source: Our MS/MS analysis indicated that GSK3β K150 and K183 residues are acetylated and GSK3β K183 is involved in the regulation of its kinase activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GSK3β K183 is involved in the regulation of its kinase activity.
source: Our MS/MS analysis indicated that GSK3β K150 and K183 residues are acetylated and GSK3β K183 is involved in the regulation of its kinase activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of mass spectrometry and kinase activity assays.

claim: GSK3β-K183R showed basal level acetylation, which is appreciably lower than the acetylation of wild type GSK3β.
source: Our results revealed that GSK3β-K183R showed basal level acetylation, which is appreciably lower than the acetylation of wild type GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylation assay data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: GSK3β is acetylated at multiple residues endogenously.
source: These findings confirm our observations that GSK3β is acetylated at multiple residues endogenously, and K183 residue is one among them.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that K183R mutant still shows basal acetylation.

claim: SIRT2 deacetylates the wild type GSK3β, but not GSK3β-K183R in the presence of NAD+.
source: SIRT2 deacetylates the wild type GSK3β, but not GSK3β-K183R in the presence of NAD+, indicating that K183R may be the key target residue for SIRT2 deacetylase (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro deacetylation assay data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: K183 may be the key target residue for SIRT2 deacetylase.
source: SIRT2 deacetylates the wild type GSK3β, but not GSK3β-K183R in the presence of NAD+, indicating that K183R may be the key target residue for SIRT2 deacetylase (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SIRT2 cannot deacetylate the K183R mutant.

claim: Catalytic activity of GSK3β is governed by acetylation at GSK3β K183 residue.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that catalytic activity of GSK3β is governed by acetylation at GSK3β K183 residue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing that K183 acetylation affects ATP binding and kinase activity.

claim: Acetylation inhibits the ATP binding to GSK3β.
source: As expected, we found that acetylation inhibits the ATP binding, whereas SIRT2-mediated deacetylation restores the ATP-binding ability of GSK3β (Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP binding assay data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: SIRT2-mediated deacetylation restores the ATP-binding ability of GSK3β.
source: As expected, we found that acetylation inhibits the ATP binding, whereas SIRT2-mediated deacetylation restores the ATP-binding ability of GSK3β (Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP binding assay data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: GSK3β kinase activity is inhibited by N-terminal Ser9 phosphorylation.
source: GSK3β kinase activity is known to be inhibited by N-terminal Ser9 phosphorylation (Ali et al., 2001; Song et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ali et al., 2001 and Song et al., 2015.

claim: There were no differences in the phosphorylation at Ser9 of GSK3β in control and SIRT2-deficient cardiomyocytes or hearts.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe any differences in the phosphorylation at Ser9 of GSK3β in control and SIRT2-deficient cardiomyocytes or hearts (Figure 3G and H), suggesting that the reduced activity of GSK3β is associated with acetylation, but not the phosphorylation at Ser9 residue.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The reduced activity of GSK3β is associated with acetylation, but not the phosphorylation at Ser9 residue.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe any differences in the phosphorylation at Ser9 of GSK3β in control and SIRT2-deficient cardiomyocytes or hearts (Figure 3G and H), suggesting that the reduced activity of GSK3β is associated with acetylation, but not the phosphorylation at Ser9 residue.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Ser9 phosphorylation is unchanged while acetylation is increased in SIRT2-deficient samples.

claim: The activity of GSK3β-S9A mutant was reduced almost three-folds when K183 was mutated to K183Q.
source: Our results suggest that the activity of GSK3β-S9A mutant, which is not inhibited by the Ser9 phosphorylation, was reduced almost three-folds when K183 was mutated to K183Q (Figure 3M).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: K183 residue is critical for ATP binding in constitutively active GSK3β S9A mutant.
source: These findings suggest that K183 residue is critical for ATP binding in constitutively active GSK3β S9A mutant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that K183Q mutation reduces activity of the S9A mutant.

claim: Acetylation might inhibit the activity of constitutively active GSK3β S9A mutant independent of inhibitory phosphorylation.
source: We presume that acetylation might inhibit the activity of constitutively active GSK3β S9A mutant independent of inhibitory phosphorylation, but further experiments are required to prove this assumption.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that K183Q mutation reduces activity of the S9A mutant.

claim: Markedly reduced phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216 residue was found in the cardiomyocytes or heart lysates of SIRT2-deficient mice.
source: Surprisingly, we found markedly reduced phosphorylation of GSK3β at Tyr216 residue in the cardiomyocytes or heart lysates of SIRT2-deficient mice (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Acetylation might have negative impact on the activating tyrosine phosphorylation of GSK3β.
source: These results suggest that acetylation might have negative impact on the activating tyrosine phosphorylation of GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that increased acetylation is associated with decreased Tyr216 phosphorylation.

claim: Both GSK3α and GSK3β are significantly acetylated in SIRT2-depleted cells as compared to control cells.
source: We found both GSK3α and GSK3β to be significantly acetylated in SIRT2-depleted cells as compared to control cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blotting data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Acetylation significantly reduced the activity of GSK3α.
source: Results suggest that acetylation significantly reduced the activity of GSK3α and incubation of acetylated-GSK3α with wild type SIRT2 restored its activity in an NAD+-dependent manner (Figure 4C), suggesting that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation enhances the activity of GSK3α.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Incubation of acetylated-GSK3α with wild type SIRT2 restored its activity in an NAD+-dependent manner.
source: Results suggest that acetylation significantly reduced the activity of GSK3α and incubation of acetylated-GSK3α with wild type SIRT2 restored its activity in an NAD+-dependent manner (Figure 4C), suggesting that SIRT2-mediated deacetylation enhances the activity of GSK3α.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SIRT2-mediated deacetylation enhances the activity of GSK3α.

claim: K99 and K246 are the acetylation sites in GSK3α.

claim: K246 of GSK3α is analogous to residue K183 of GSK3β.

claim: The residue K246 would occupy the same position proximal to the adenine nucleotide as K183 of GSK3β.

evidence: The claim is supported by homology modeling shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Acetylation of residue K246 would play a similar role in de-stabilizing adenine nucleotide in the pocket of GSK3α.
source: We therefore assume that acetylation of residue K246 would play a similar role in de-stabilizing adenine nucleotide in the pocket of GSK3α.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the structural similarity between K246 in GSK3α and K183 in GSK3β.

claim: Activation of GSK3β antagonizes the development of cardiac hypertrophy.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Antos et al., 2002; Kerkela et al., 2008; and Sugden et al., 2008.

claim: Cardiac myocyte-specific deletion of GSK3α and GSK3β, together, results in severe dilated cardiomyopathy.

claim: Acetylation of GSK3 isoforms is a novel post-translational modification which hinders the ATP binding.

evidence: The claim is supported by ATP binding assays and kinase activity assays throughout the manuscript.
